title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: six intelligences and one draft

questions.prompt: Amine is nine. He finished the whole maths book of the year in October and asked for the next one. Which word of the lesson names a child like him?

options.text: a gift
a prodigy
curiosity
a brain

questions.explanation: "a prodigy" is the word: it names a young person whose ability astonishes people, and the age is part of the meaning. "a brain" is the organ he thinks with, "curiosity" is the wish that pushed him to ask for the next book, and "a gift" is the ability itself and not the child who carries it. Only one of the four names a person.

questions.prompt: The questionnaire sorts its questions into six sets, one for each type of intelligence. What is a pupil supposed to find out by answering it?

options.text: how many of the questions he can answer with a yes
which pupil of the class is the most intelligent of all
which school subject he should choose next year
which type or types of intelligence are his own

questions.explanation: "which type or types of intelligence are his own" is the aim: the six sets are six doors, not a ladder, and a pupil may well come out with two or three. "which pupil of the class is the most intelligent of all" turns the lesson into a competition it refuses. "how many of the questions he can answer with a yes" counts instead of sorting, and "which school subject he should choose next year" is a decision the questionnaire never claims to make.

questions.prompt: You have chosen your statements, found your examples, added the age, the appearance and the background, and written a first draft. What does the lesson ask you to do next?

options.text: Choose the statements that apply to your person.
Copy it neatly into your notebook and hand it in.
Exchange it with a partner and read his draft too.
Look for three more gifted people to describe.

questions.explanation: "Exchange it with a partner and read his draft too." is the next move: the draft exists to be read by somebody else, who then suggests improvements on the ideas, the grammar and the vocabulary. "Copy it neatly into your notebook and hand it in." skips that reading altogether. The classic trap is "Choose the statements that apply to your person.", which is the very first move of all, already done, and "Look for three more gifted people to describe." invents work the lesson never asks for.

questions.prompt: At the end of the text the writer claims that gifts are not rare at all. Which sentence says the same thing?

options.text: Almost every young person has a gift of his own.
Gifts belong to the pupils who pass every exam.
Only a few children in a country are ever gifted.
A gift can be bought with enough money and work.

questions.explanation: "Almost every young person has a gift of his own." carries the writer's idea: the gift is spread widely, and what changes from one child to the next is its kind, not its existence. "Only a few children in a country are ever gifted." says exactly the opposite. "A gift can be bought with enough money and work." contradicts the word natural, and "Gifts belong to the pupils who pass every exam." is the narrow definition the whole lesson argues against.

questions.prompt: Rym repairs the school's broken chairs herself, and the younger pupils come to her with their worries because she listens to them. Which two intelligences does she show?

options.text: artistic and social
emotional and artistic
mechanical and physical
mechanical and social

questions.explanation: "mechanical and social" is the pair: repairing a broken object is the mechanical sign, and listening to what others feel is the social one. "mechanical and physical" would need sport or energy, which nothing in the sentence gives. "artistic and social" and "emotional and artistic" both bring in words or pictures, and Rym neither draws nor writes here. Read each half of the sentence and give it its own type.

questions.prompt: Nour writes this acrostic: "Playing in the school yard / Understanding new lessons / Painting in the art room / I like reading books / Learning new words / Singing in the big choir." One line breaks the rule of the poem. Which one is it?

options.text: I like reading books
Playing in the school yard
Singing in the big choir
Understanding new lessons

questions.explanation: "I like reading books" is the faulty line: every line of an acrostic opens with a verb in the -ing form, and this one opens with a subject followed by a conjugated verb. Its first letter is right, which is what makes it hard to see: the six initials still spell PUPILS. The trap is the word reading, an -ing form that arrives too late in the line to save it. The three other lines all begin with their -ing verb.
